meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Don't give up. Don't ever give up.'?
meta.ogDescription: Jim Valvano said it on 4 March 1993, eight weeks before he died, announcing the V Foundation for Cancer Research. Here’s the sentence it actually sits in.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: Valvano said it on 4 March 1993, accepting the first Arthur Ashe Courage and Humanitarian Award at the first ESPY Awards, while announcing what he called the Jimmy V Foundation for Cancer Research (today the V Foundation for Cancer Research). His actual sentence was ‘And its motto is, “Don’t give up. Don’t ever give up.”’ — the words were the foundation’s motto before they were a quotation.

source.excerpt: And its motto is, “Don’t give up. Don’t ever give up.”
trail: The speech is on the record twice over: ESPN’s video of the 1993 ESPY speech ↗, and ESPN’s own annotated transcript ↗.
Independent transcripts agree on the wording, including the one at James Clear’s speech archive ↗ and Rev’s ↗.

Wikipedia ↗ confirms the occasion only: the inaugural Arthur Ashe Courage Award was given to Valvano at the 1993 ESPYs. The foundation announcement is in the speech itself — ESPN’s annotated transcript carries ‘We are starting the Jimmy V Foundation for Cancer Research. And its motto is…’

The V Foundation ↗ still carries the line as its motto — its About page prints it as a registered mark, ‘Don’t Give Up . . . Don’t Ever Give Up!’® — which is the strongest kind of corroboration available: the organisation the sentence was written for has used it continuously ever since.
source.cutTag: ↑ the six famous words are a quotation inside a quotation — he was reading out a motto, not addressing the room
source.excerptNote: Punctuation varies: ESPN’s transcript prints it with an ellipsis, ‘Don’t give up ... don’t ever give up’, some outlets use a comma, and the V Foundation’s registered mark is ‘Don’t Give Up . . . Don’t Ever Give Up!’® The words are identical in every version.

source.rightsNote: The speech was delivered in 1993 and is firmly in copyright — nowhere near the pre-1931 threshold for the public domain — and the broadcast is ESPN’s. The motto is also the working slogan of the V Foundation, a live charitable trademark. The line is quoted here for identification and verification; do not treat the speech as free to reproduce.

author.name: Jim Valvano
author.heading: About Jim Valvano
author.bio: Jim Valvano coached North Carolina State from 1980 to 1990 and is best remembered for 1983, when a team nobody rated beat Houston for the national championship and he ran around the floor looking for someone to hug. He moved to broadcasting with ESPN and ABC afterwards and won a CableACE award for it. In June 1992 he was diagnosed with metastatic cancer. He gave this speech nine months later and died on 28 April 1993, aged 47 — eight weeks after founding the charity that now carries the line.

context.heading: Why it matters
lead: Valvano was dying when he said it. He had been given a year the previous summer, he had trouble getting out of his seat, and a screen in front of him was flashing ‘30 seconds’ at him to wrap up. He ignored it, talked for around ten minutes, and used the time to announce that he was starting a foundation to fund cancer research.

The six words are the foundation’s motto, spoken at the moment it was launched — which is why they carry more freight than a slogan should. He was not telling an audience of athletes to try harder. He was describing the terms on which he intended to spend the eight weeks he had left.
context.detailsSummary: The line people usually pair it with
detailsBody: The other famous passage from the same speech is the one about what cancer could and could not take — his body, but not his mind, his heart or his soul. The two are often quoted together, and they come from the same ten minutes.

The V Foundation for Cancer Research still exists and still uses the motto; by its own count ↗ it has awarded nearly $458 million in research funding to more than 1,400 grantees. The line stayed in circulation because an institution kept saying it, not only because the speech was moving.
context.pull: He was not telling athletes to try harder. He was setting the terms for the eight weeks he had left.
